chapterTitle: Ultra-Low-Latency Messaging: Aeron and Chronicle Queue

parts.partTitle: Why TCP and HTTP Kill Your Trading Engine

beats.headline: Why is your 5-millisecond latency a failure?
beats.subline: In electronic trading, 5 milliseconds is an eternity. Standard TCP and kernel networking are your biggest enemies.
beats.narration: In microservices, five milliseconds is fast. In electronic trading, it is a disaster. If you use TCP or standard socket calls, you are already losing the race to the kernel.

beats.title: TCP vs. Aeron UDP Multicast

top.label: Standard TCP
points: One dropped packet stalls the whole stream

beats.narration: TCP enforces ordered delivery. If one packet drops, the kernel buffers everything behind it, spiking latency. Aeron uses UDP multicast, letting switches replicate data in hardware with zero skew.

beats.title: Aeron Media Driver Architecture
beats.subtitle: Isolating I/O from Business Logic

nodes.label: Business Thread
nodes.detail: Polls/Offers to shared memory log buffers

nodes.label: Media Driver
nodes.detail: Pinned threads handling NIC I/O and NAKs

beats.narration: The Media Driver runs on its own pinned core. It handles the network, while your business thread simply reads and writes to pre-allocated shared memory buffers. No syscalls, no heap allocation.

beats.title: Non-blocking Publication

steps.explanation: Atomic tail increment on memory-mapped file. Zero system calls.
Explicit flow control. Never block the thread; just retry.

beats.narration: Notice the return codes. We never block. If the receiver is slow, we get back-pressured and spin, keeping our hot path clean and predictable.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Chronicle Queue for sub-microsecond IPC →
beats.narration: Aeron handles the network. In Part 2, we look at Chronicle Queue for ultra-fast inter-process communication on the same machine.

beats.headline: Why use localhost TCP for IPC?
beats.subline: It is a massive waste of cycles. Map your memory directly to bypass the kernel entirely.
beats.narration: If two processes on the same host talk over localhost TCP, you are hitting the kernel stack for no reason. Chronicle Queue maps files directly into memory for sub-microsecond handoffs.

beats.title: Chronicle Queue Memory Mapping
beats.subtitle: Shared memory via POSIX mmap

nodes.label: OS Page Cache
nodes.detail: Shared memory visible to both processes

beats.narration: Chronicle Queue uses mmap to share memory pages between processes. The OS page cache handles the heavy lifting, and the data is persisted to disk asynchronously.

beats.title: Zero-Allocation Appender

steps.explanation: Manages the memory lock and header commit atomically.
Binary encoding directly into the shared memory page.

beats.narration: We use DocumentContext to write structured data. It encodes directly into the memory page, meaning zero garbage collection during your hot trading loop.

beats.title: Persistence Options
beats.caption: Where does your data live?
beats.narration: Use NVMe for audit trails and crash recovery. Use /dev/shm for pure RAM speed when you don't care about persistence after a reboot.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Choose storage based on persistence needs
beats.narration: You have the transport and the IPC. In Part 3, we bypass the Linux network stack entirely using Solarflare OpenOnload.

beats.headline: The kernel is your bottleneck.
beats.subline: Interrupts and context switches are killing your performance. Move the NIC into user space.
beats.narration: Even with Aeron, the Linux kernel stack is a bottleneck. Interrupts and buffer copies add microseconds. We need to move the NIC driver into user space.

beats.title: Standard vs. Kernel Bypass
beats.subtitle: Removing the Kernel from the path
beats.narration: Kernel bypass maps NIC hardware rings directly to user space. No interrupts, no context switches. We poll the NIC directly from our application thread.

beats.title: Launching with OpenOnload
beats.caption: Intercepting standard sockets
beats.narration: Solarflare OpenOnload intercepts your standard socket calls. You don't even need to change your Java code. Just launch with the onload wrapper and pin your threads.

beats.title: OpenOnload vs. DPDK
beats.narration: OpenOnload is the gold standard for compatibility. DPDK is for when you need absolute control and are willing to write custom drivers.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: We have the hardware speed. In Part 4, we design the matching engine using deterministic event sourcing.

beats.headline: Why non-deterministic code is a bug.
beats.subline: If your matching engine calls System.nanoTime(), you can never reproduce a production race condition.
beats.narration: If your matching engine calls system time or random numbers, you can't replay it. Determinism is the only way to guarantee your engine is bug-free.

beats.title: Deterministic Matching Engine
beats.subtitle: Journaling as the source of truth
beats.narration: Journal the input first. The matching core is a pure function of that journal. Same input, same output, every single time. Perfect for debugging.

beats.title: The Deterministic Loop

steps.explanation: Use the timestamp from the gateway. Never call System.nanoTime() here.
The order book state is entirely derived from the input sequence.

beats.narration: Notice we don't call time inside the loop. We use the time stamped at the gateway. This keeps the engine pure and replayable.

beats.title: The Payoff
beats.caption: Why this architecture wins
beats.narration: This architecture gives you disaster recovery and perfect bug reproduction. You get the speed of a single thread with the safety of a distributed system.
